items.q: You are to design a VR training simulator for firefighters to prepare for a high-risk indoor rescue mission. Outline your approach in a way that demonstrates cognitive load, realism, system performance trade-offs and safety implications of training in a high-fidelity VR environment.
items.answer:
Structure the answer around the **four dimensions the question names**.

**1. Why VR at all**
Firefighting training needs **danger without risk** — the second of the three things VR uniquely offers (scale, danger, impossibility). A burning building can be rehearsed a hundred times; a real one cannot.

**2. Realism — what must be high fidelity, and what need not be**

| Must be faithful | Can be abstracted |
|---|---|
| **Spatial layout** — the actual building geometry; the trainee must build a real mental map | Photoreal textures on distant surfaces |
| **Smoke behaviour and visibility** — the core perceptual challenge | Individual flame particles |
| **Audio** — alarms, structural noise, voices; **spatial audio** for locating a casualty | Full acoustic simulation |
| **Procedure and equipment handling** | Facial detail on NPCs (**uncanny valley** — a stylised casualty avoids it) |

**3. Cognitive load**
The purpose is to make procedure **automatic under stress**, so the simulator must load the trainee deliberately:
- **Intrinsic load** — the task itself (navigate, search, extract). Keep this.
- **Extraneous load** — awkward controls, menu diving, unclear affordances. **Eliminate this** — every unit of attention spent fighting the interface is not spent learning.
- **Germane load** — building the mental schema. Support with **after-action review** rather than in-scene hints.

Practical consequences: **diegetic UI** (information on the equipment, not floating menus), **no reading** under time pressure, and **progressive difficulty** — layout first, then smoke, then time pressure, then casualties.

**4. System performance trade-offs**

| Requirement | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| **Motion-to-photon < 20 ms** | Non-negotiable — the VOR sets it. Cut scene complexity before latency. |
| **Stable 90 fps** | **Consistency beats peak** — an oscillating rate is itself a sickness trigger. Budget for the worst case (heavy smoke) not the average. |
| **Stereoscopic rendering** | Everything is drawn **twice** — roughly half the polygon budget of a flat screen. |
| **Volumetric smoke** | The most expensive effect and the most important one. Spend here; use **foveated rendering** if eye tracking is available. |
| **Tracking** | **Room-scale inside-out (SLAM)** — trainees must physically crawl and move; a tethered outside-in rig is a trip hazard. |

**5. Safety implications**
- **Physical:** trainees move while blind to the real room. Requires **guardian bounds**, a clear physical space, a spotter, and heavy real equipment omitted or mocked.
- **Simulator sickness:** use **physical locomotion**, not artificial; avoid unrequested camera motion, which is the strongest nausea trigger.
- **Psychological:** high-presence VR produces **genuine fear responses** — that is the point, but it demands consent, an immediate exit, and debriefing.
- **Negative transfer — the most important risk:** if the simulator lets trainees do something that would kill them in reality (walk through fire without consequence, ignore air supply), it **trains the wrong reflex**. Fidelity of *consequence* matters more than fidelity of *pixels*.

**Conclusion:** the design principle is **fidelity where it changes behaviour, abstraction everywhere else** — and latency and frame-rate stability are constraints, not variables.

items.q: What are the different eye movements? Explain each with examples.
items.answer:
| Movement | What it does | Speed / range | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Saccade** | **Rapid ballistic jump** repositioning the fovea onto a new target; cannot be corrected mid-flight | up to **900°/s**, 20–200 ms | Reading — your eyes jump 3–4 times a second, they do not sweep |
| **Smooth pursuit** | **Smoothly tracks a moving target** to hold it on the fovea; impossible without a target | up to **~30°/s** | Following a bird across the sky |
| **Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR)** | Eyes **counter-rotate against head motion** to hold gaze; driven by the **inner ear** | **~10 ms latency** | Fix your gaze on a word and shake your head — it stays readable |
| **Optokinetic Reflex (OKR)** | Tracks a **large moving field**; slow drift then fast reset (**optokinetic nystagmus**) | — | Looking out of a moving train |
| **Vergence** | Eyes rotate in **opposite** directions to fixate at a depth — the only non-conjugate movement | close range | Bringing a finger toward your nose |
| **Microsaccades** | Tiny involuntary tremor during fixation | **< 1°** | Prevents **perceptual fading** — a perfectly stabilised image disappears within seconds |

**The implications for VR** — this is what turns a list into a full answer:

1. **VOR ⇒ the latency budget.** The reflex responds in ~10 ms and is calibrated to a perfectly stable world. If the display lags, the eyes compensate correctly but the image has not updated, so the world **slips across the retina** — sensory conflict and **motion sickness**. This is why **motion-to-photon must stay under ~20 ms**, forcing 90 fps, pose prediction and late-stage reprojection.
2. **Smooth pursuit ⇒ low-persistence displays.** A sample-and-hold panel smears a static image across the moving retina (**judder**). Illuminating each frame for only **1–2 ms** fixes it.
3. **The fovea (~2°) ⇒ foveated rendering.** Full resolution only around the gaze point saves **50–70%** of shading cost.
4. **Saccadic suppression ⇒ redirected walking.** Vision is suppressed during a jump, so the world can be subtly rotated unnoticed.
5. **Vergence ⇒ the vergence–accommodation conflict.** Vergence varies with virtual depth while focus is fixed at the screen — causing **eye strain**, the deepest unsolved problem in headset design.

items.q: What is perception, and what is the importance of perception in visual realism?
items.answer:
**Perception** is the process by which the brain **interprets and organises sensory input into a model of the world**. It is **not** a faithful recording — it is an **active reconstruction** that fills gaps, resolves ambiguity and discards most of the incoming signal.

**Why this matters for visual realism:** the target of a graphics system is **not physical accuracy but perceptual sufficiency**. You do not need to reproduce the light field; you need to supply the cues the visual system actually uses.

**The depth cues that carry realism**, roughly in order of usefulness:

| Cue | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Occlusion** | Monocular | The **strongest** cue — and the one **OST displays cannot provide** |
| **Perspective / relative size** | Monocular | Delivered by the projection matrix (Unit 2) |
| **Motion parallax** | Monocular, dynamic | Requires **6DOF tracking** — nearer things move more |
| **Shading and shadows** | Monocular | Contact shadows especially anchor objects to surfaces |
| **Stereopsis** | Binocular | Disparity between the two eyes; the reason for stereoscopic rendering |
| **Vergence & accommodation** | Oculomotor | The pair that **conflict** in a headset |

**Three consequences for design:**

1. **You can spend selectively.** Since only ~2° of the field is high-acuity, **foveated rendering** discards detail nobody can see. Since occlusion dominates, getting depth ordering right matters more than adding polygons.
2. **Consistency matters more than fidelity.** A stylised world with **coherent** cues reads as more real than a photoreal one where shadows disagree with lighting — this is also the **uncanny valley** in one sentence.
3. **A missing or contradictory cue is worse than a crude one.** No shadow makes an object float; a virtual object that fails to be occluded by a real wall destroys the illusion instantly. **Perceptual realism is limited by the weakest cue, not the strongest.**

**Conclusion:** understanding perception tells you **where to spend and where to cheat** — which is the whole economics of real-time graphics.

The **uncanny valley** is the observed **drop in human affinity** for a virtual character (or robot) as it becomes **almost — but not quite — human-like**.

```
  affinity
     ▲
     │      ╭──╮                        ╭─── healthy human
     │     ╱    ╲                      ╱
     │    ╱      ╲                    ╱
     │   ╱        ╲______________   ╱
     │  ╱                        ╲╱
     └────────────────────────────────▶  human likeness
                         ▲
                  the uncanny valley
```

- As human likeness increases, affinity **rises** — a stylised cartoon character is appealing.
- Just short of realism, affinity **collapses**: small imperfections in **skin, eye movement, facial timing or gait** read as *wrong* rather than *stylised*. The result feels unsettling, even corpse-like.
- Affinity recovers only at **genuine realism**.

**Why it happens (the leading explanation):** once a figure is close enough to human, the brain stops evaluating it as an *artefact* and starts evaluating it as a *person* — and then applies the extremely sensitive machinery it uses to detect illness, deception and death. Small errors become alarming rather than charming.

**The practical lesson for VR — and this is the examinable part:**

> **A deliberately stylised avatar is often more comfortable than a nearly-photoreal one.** Aiming at realism and missing lands you in the valley; staying deliberately to the left of it does not.

This is why many social VR platforms use **abstract or cartoon avatars**, and why the course lists the uncanny valley alongside motion sickness as one of the **two named challenges of VR development**. **Motion is the harder half** — a still render may escape the valley while the same character in motion falls straight into it, because timing errors are more detectable than static ones.

items.q: Explain the different augmentation techniques adopted in an augmented reality application.
items.answer:
**Augmentation technique** = how the virtual content is delivered to the user's senses and anchored to the world. Three ways to classify them.

**A. By display technology** (the spatial display models):

| Technique | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Optical see-through** | Real world seen **directly** through a semi-transparent combiner; virtual content projected onto it | **HoloLens** |
| **Video see-through** | Cameras capture the world, virtual content is **composited**, result shown on internal screens | **Quest 3** passthrough |
| **Spatial projection** | Images projected **directly onto physical surfaces** — no headset | **CAVE**, projection mapping |
| **Handheld / magic lens** | The device screen acts as a window onto the augmented world | Phone AR, **Pokémon GO** |

**B. By how content is anchored** (the registration technique):

| Technique | How the anchor is found | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Marker-based** | A **fiducial pattern** of known geometry is detected in the image | Accurate and simple, but the environment must be **prepared** |
| **Markerless / natural feature** | **Corners, edges and textures** already in the scene are detected and tracked | No preparation, but computationally heavy and can **drift** |
| **Model-based** | A known 3D CAD model of the object is matched against the image | Excellent for industrial parts; needs the model |
| **Location-based** | **GPS + compass** place content geographically | Works outdoors at scale; only **1–100 m** accurate — coarse |
| **SLAM-based** | The device **builds a map** of the room and localises within it | Robust and unprepared; the modern default |

**C. By reference frame** (where the content sits):

- **World-fixed** — anchored to the environment; requires full 6DOF registration.
- **User-fixed** — head-, torso- or hand-referenced; moves with the user, needs little tracking.

**Beyond vision.** AR is defined by its **three requirements**, not by a display, so augmentation also includes:
- **Audio AR** — spatially registered sound (a voice apparently from a real location);
- **Haptic AR** — force or tactile feedback registered to real objects.

**Conclusion:** choosing a technique means choosing where to sit on three axes — **how the light reaches the eye** (OST/VST/projection/handheld), **how the anchor is found** (marker/markerless/model/location/SLAM) and **what the content is fixed to** (world or user).

items.q: What is a Virtual World Generator? Explain the details of hardware and software.
items.answer:
**The Virtual World Generator (VWG)** is the **core application layer** of a VR/AR system. It:
- **manages the state and behaviour of virtual objects**;
- **simulates environmental physics** — gravity, collisions, material interactions;
- **coordinates interactions** between the virtual environment and tracked user actions.

*Example:* in a VR training simulator the VWG manages **object positions, character behaviour and real-time scenario progression** based on user input.

> The VWG is **the authority on what is true** in the virtual world. It does not draw and it does not read sensors — it owns the **state**.

**The three software modules and how they fit together:**

| Module | Owns | Responsibilities |
|---|---|---|
| **Virtual World Generator** | **State** | Object behaviour, physics simulation, interaction coordination |
| **Rendering engine** | **Pixels** | **Stereoscopic rendering** (one image per eye), real-time lighting and shading, **optimised frames at 60–120 fps** to prevent motion sickness. *Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 5* |
| **Input processing system** | **Intent** | Handles motion controllers, hand tracking, voice recognition, traditional controllers; **queues, prioritises and interprets** input to update the world in real time |

```
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                              │
  ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌───────────────────┐
  │   VWG     │───▶│  RENDERING   │───▶│  user sees it     │
  │  (state,  │    │   ENGINE     │    └───────────────────┘
  │  physics) │    └──────────────┘              │ user acts
  └───────────┘◀───┌──────────────┐◀─────────────┘
                   │    INPUT     │
                   └──────────────┘
```

**The hardware it runs on:**

| Group | Components |
|---|---|
| **Displays** | **OST HMD** (HoloLens) · **VST HMD** (Rift, Vive, Quest) · **spatial projection** (CAVE) |
| **Sensors** | **IMU** = gyroscope + accelerometer + magnetometer · **GPS** (1–100 m, sub-metre with **DGPS**) · **external tracking** (Lighthouse base stations) |
| **Computing** | **High-performance GPUs** · **tethered** systems (Rift, Vive Pro) for fidelity · **mobile/standalone** (Google Cardboard, Meta Quest 3) for portability |

**The constraint that ties it together:** the loop must complete within the **motion-to-photon budget of roughly 20 ms**, because the **vestibulo-ocular reflex** responds in ~10 ms and expects a perfectly stable world. Exceed it and you get registration error in AR and **motion sickness** in VR.

> Note this is the **modelling–rendering paradigm** of Unit 2 with a third module added: modeller → interface file → renderer becomes **VWG → scene state → rendering engine**, and what is new is the **input system closing the loop**. That loop is the whole difference between watching and being present.

items.q: What does tracking in a 3D environment mean? What are the various types of tracking?
items.answer:
**Definition.** Tracking is determining, **in real time**, the **position and orientation** — the **6DOF pose** — of users, controllers and objects relative to a physical or virtual environment. It is what makes virtual content stay aligned with the real world (**registration**) and what makes a VR viewpoint follow the head.

**A pose** is $(\mathbf p, q)$: position $\mathbf p \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and orientation as a **unit quaternion** $q$ — equivalently a $4\times4$ homogeneous matrix.

**The four technologies:**

| | **Mechanical** | **Electromagnetic** | **Ultrasonic** | **Optical** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Principle** | Articulated linkages with **joint angle sensors** | Base station generates a **magnetic field**; sensors measure strength and orientation | **Time-of-flight** of sound between transmitters and microphones | **Cameras** track markers or natural features |
| **Advantages** | **Very high precision, low latency**; reliable in fixed environments | **No line-of-sight** needed; tracks **through obstructions** | **Low cost**; good in small enclosed spaces | High accuracy; **no infrastructure** for markerless |
| **Limitations** | **Limited DOF**; user **tethered** | **Sensitive to metal and EM interference**; limited range | **Noise and reflections**; limited range; **slow update rate** | Needs **line of sight**; **lighting-dependent**; markerless may **drift** |
| **Example** | Medical simulators | **Polhemus** | Early VR head trackers | **ARToolKit**, Vuforia, ARKit |

**Within optical, the key subdivision:**
- **Marker-based** — **fiducial markers** (ARToolKit) of known geometry; **accurate and reliable in controlled environments**, but requires clear line of sight, good lighting, and someone to **place the markers**.
- **Markerless / natural feature** — detects **corners, edges and textures** already present, using **SLAM** and **NFT**; works in **unprepared, dynamic environments** but is **computationally intensive**, lighting-dependent and prone to **drift**.

**Other useful classifications to mention:**
- **Outside-in** (fixed sensors watch the device — Lighthouse) vs **inside-out** (the device watches the room — Quest, HoloLens).
- **3DOF** (orientation only — Google Cardboard) vs **6DOF** (adds position).

**How trackers are judged:** accuracy, **precision/jitter**, **latency**, update rate, **drift**, working volume, line-of-sight requirement and interference susceptibility.

**Conclusion:** every method trades off **precision, mobility, cost and susceptibility to interference**, and **no single technology wins on every axis** — which is why real systems **combine several through sensor fusion**.

items.q: How do you represent the pose of a rigid body that is subjected to tracking, mathematically?
items.answer:
**A pose is position and orientation together — six degrees of freedom.**

| | Degrees of freedom |
|---|---|
| **Position (translation)** | surge ($x$), sway ($y$), heave ($z$) — **3** |
| **Orientation (rotation)** | roll, pitch, yaw — **3** |

**Representation 1 — position vector plus unit quaternion**

$$\text{pose} = (\mathbf p,\ q), \qquad \mathbf p = (x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3, \qquad q = (w,x,y,z),\ \lVert q\rVert = 1$$

**Why a quaternion rather than Euler angles:**
- **No gimbal lock** — Euler angles lose a degree of freedom when the middle rotation reaches ±90°;
- **compact** — 4 numbers versus a matrix's 9;
- **smoothly interpolatable** via **slerp**, at constant angular velocity;
- **cheap to compose** — successive rotations multiply, and **re-normalisation** keeps it valid.

**Representation 2 — a homogeneous transformation matrix**

$$T = \begin{bmatrix} R_{3\times3} & \mathbf p \\ \mathbf 0^{\mathsf T} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

where $R$ is the rotation matrix equivalent to $q$. This is the body's **frame expressed in the world frame** — precisely Unit 2's **model matrix**. Composing poses along a chain of attached bodies is then matrix multiplication:

$$T^{\text{world}}_{\text{hand}} = T^{\text{world}}_{\text{shoulder}}\; T^{\text{shoulder}}_{\text{upper}}\; T^{\text{upper}}_{\text{fore}}\; T^{\text{fore}}_{\text{hand}}$$

**How the pose is maintained over time.** The tracker delivers a stream of poses; orientation is updated from the gyroscope by composing **incremental rotation quaternions**:

$$\Delta q = \left(\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2},\ \hat{\mathbf u}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right), \qquad \theta = \lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert\,\Delta t, \qquad \hat{\mathbf u} = \frac{\boldsymbol\omega}{\lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert}$$

$$q_{k+1} = q_k \otimes \Delta q_k \qquad\text{(body frame)}$$

followed by **re-normalisation** $q \leftarrow q/\lVert q\rVert$ to prevent floating-point drift.

**Note on convention.** State whether $q$ is written $(w,x,y,z)$ or $(x,y,z,w)$ — both appear in this course — and whether composition is body-frame ($q\otimes\Delta q$) or global-frame ($\Delta q\otimes q$). Marks are lost more often to unstated conventions than to arithmetic.
